passage:
Monday, 11 am
Alka: Hi Jasleen, quick one. Pune client or Jaipur client first?
Jasleen: What are you leaning towards?
Alka: honestly no idea. just tell me and I'll do it 😅
Jasleen: I could. But I won't be on those calls, you will
Alka: I'm scared of picking wrong
Jasleen: Fair. Try this: two lines on why each one, then tell me what you'd choose
Alka: ok... Pune. bigger renewal and the contact already knows me
Jasleen: That's a solid reason. Go with it
Alka: wait, so you agree?
Jasleen: I agree that you HAVE a reason. Tell me on Friday how it went 🙂
Alka: ok. doing it

qa.q: Which client does Alka choose to start with?
Why does Alka want Jasleen to just decide?
qa.a: Alka is scared of picking wrong and would like Jasleen to carry the decision.

qa.q: How does Jasleen help Alka build judgment rather than dependence?
qa.a: Jasleen asks Alka to write two lines of reasons, then choose, and asks for a report on Friday.

qa.q: Why might Jasleen refuse to simply give the answer?
qa.a: Jasleen will not be on the calls, so Alka needs the confidence to decide and to trust their own judgment.

grounding: A mentee keeps asking a mentor to decide for them out of fear of mistakes, and the mentor steers them toward making their own decision.

passage:
Zubin, you call your mentor before choosing a shirt. Sit down. Your Nirmala aunty was worse.

At twenty-four I joined a publishing house, and Mrs. Anand took me under her wing. She was so wise that I stopped thinking. Which manuscript to read first? I asked her. Whether to take a day off? I asked her. Once I even asked which pen to buy.

One day she was away in Delhi, and a writer called wanting an answer on his contract by evening. I sat there frozen, sweating, terrified of choosing wrong.

When Mrs. Anand came back, I expected praise for waiting. Instead she said, very gently, "Nirmala, I don't want to be your brain. I want to be your sounding board."

That was the turning point. From then on I made small decisions myself and brought her only the big ones, with my own view first. "Here's what I think. What am I missing?" She smiled every time.

qa.q: Where was Mrs. Anand when the writer called?
How did young Nirmala feel when she had to answer the writer alone?
qa.a: She felt frozen and terrified, sweating with fear of choosing wrong.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nirmala's story?
qa.a: Mrs. Anand told her she wanted to be a sounding board, not her brain, so Nirmala began making small decisions herself and bringing her own view first.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Anand seem to feel about Nirmala's dependence?
qa.a: Mrs. Anand seemed gently concerned, wanting Nirmala to trust her own judgment rather than rely on her for everything.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young woman who asked her mentor to decide everything out of fear of mistakes, and who learned to take small decisions and ask for perspective, not answers.

passage:
The vendor needed an answer by four, and Suraj, Vaibhav's mentor, was on a flight to Singapore with his phone off. Vaibhav stared at the two quotes on his screen. For a year he had run every decision past Suraj: which supplier, which font, which reply. He had never once gone first.

His palms were damp. What if he picked the wrong one and cost the company?

He made himself do what Suraj always did. He wrote down price, delivery time, and past quality for both vendors. The cheaper one had missed two deadlines last year. The other was slightly more expensive but reliable.

At three-forty he signed with the reliable one and emailed Suraj: "Chose Vendor B for reliability; here's my reasoning. Would you have done anything differently?"

Suraj replied that night from the airport. "Same choice. Next time, don't even ask me. Just tell me." Vaibhav read it three times, grinning.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling as he looked at the two quotes?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt anxious, with damp palms, afraid of choosing wrong and costing the company.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do instead of waiting for Suraj?
qa.a: He weighed the options using Suraj's method, made the decision himself, and asked Suraj for perspective afterwards rather than for the answer.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel about Vaibhav's decision?
qa.a: Suraj was pleased and trusting, telling Vaibhav he no longer needed to ask first.

grounding: The story shows a young man who asked his mentor to decide everything out of fear of mistakes, who takes a decision himself and asks for perspective, building trust in his own judgment.
